requirement:
# REQ-2129: Feature Request: Allow generation of Formatter for a type in a referenced assembly

Source: https://github.com/MessagePack-CSharp/MessagePack-CSharp/issues/2129

## Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

Given the following project structure:

 - Project A
    - `ProjectA.MyType`

 - Project B
    - References
        - Project A
    - Package References
        - MessagePack
    
I need to have a source-generated `IMessagePackFormatter` for type `ProjectA.MyType` generated **inside Project B** instead of Project A, because the latter has no (and cannot have) reference to MessagePack nuget package.

## Describe the solution you'd like

Add a `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]` attribute that will work for partial classes implementing `IMessagePackFormatter<T>`.

For example:

```csharp
[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]
partial class MyObjectFormatter: IMessagePackFormatter<MyObject>;
```

That's it. The class does not even need to declare a body (no `{` and `}`), because the actual implementation is source-generated by `MessagePack.SourceGenerator.MessagePackGenerator` as usual.

As for the attribute-based property keys and other settings (such as Union), I can think of 3 alternatives:

1 - Use `System.Runtime.Serialization.DataMember` and related attributes. This is too limited IMO, as it cannot have `Union` and other features.

2 - Allow the generator and analyzers to work with user-defined versions of the MessagePack attributes. This would be similar to how you can declare dummy versions of BCL attributes that the C# compiler expects, such as [`[IsExternalInit]`](https://stackoverflow.com/a/67687186/643085) or `[ModuleInitializer]`. With this, I could simply copy and paste the attribute definitions for MessagePack attributes such as `[Key]` into my Project A, and have the source-generated formatter (as described above) pick them.

3 - Source-generate the attributes themselves using [`IncrementalGeneratorInitializationContext.RegisterPostInitializationOutput`](https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/blob/main/docs/features/incremental-generators.md#outputting-values) instead of them existing in the `MessagePack.Annotations` assembly. This would allow using the attributes without adding an additional runtime dependency. Only compile-time reference to the analyzer Nuget would be required.

## Motivation

Project A is really a library (Nuget package), and I really want to keep it minimal. It currently has zero dependencies and I would really like to keep it that way.

story.summary: Adds a public `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]` attribute to MessagePack.Annotations. A user marks a `partial` class that implements `IMessagePackFormatter<T>` with it, and the source generator writes the formatter body into that class and registers it in `GeneratedMessagePackResolver`. `T` can come from an assembly with no MessagePack reference. By default, `T` is serialized contractless: public read-write instance members, in name order, under string keys. An optional `SurrogateType` names another type whose `[Key]`/`[IgnoreMember]` attributes set the keys and which members are included. Four new error diagnostics (MsgPack019–022) cover misuse. Both formatter templates now emit `partial class` instead of `internal sealed class` for these user-declared formatters.

findings.description: Claim C5 disputed: First, it does not serialize every public read-write property across base types: in GeneratedFormatterCollector.cs lines 279-281, IsPublicReadWrite checks property.GetMethod and property.SetMethod directly on the derived IPropertySymbol without walking OverriddenProperty. In Roslyn (especially for external assembly metadata symbols), a derived override that overrides only get has SetMethod == null (and one overriding only set has GetMethod == null); because line 267 adds the name to seen, both the derived and base symbols are skipped and the public read-write property is silently dropped. Second, none of the four named tests exercise base types or member hiding.

Claim C7 disputed: First, selecting formatterInterfaces[0] happens on line 63 of GeneratedFormatterCollector.cs, outside the cited lines 53-61. Second, if there are several IMessagePackFormatter<T> interfaces on an empty partial class, the first is not 'used silently'—compilation fails with CS0535 because the remaining IMessagePackFormatter<T> interfaces are left unimplemented, and no test covers multiple formatter interfaces.

Claim C8 disputed: The named test FormattedTypeMustNotBeAbstract (GeneratedMessagePackFormatterTests.cs lines 78-102) only tests an abstract data type (MsgPack021). Neither it nor any other test in the change tests generic types, inaccessible types, or the NoDeserializingConstructor diagnostic path at GeneratedFormatterCollector.cs lines 77-81.

Claim C9 disputed: Callback-receiver support in GeneratedFormatterCollector.cs lines 84-85 is broken for explicit interface implementations and untested by the named tests. In Roslyn, an explicit interface implementation method has a qualified IMethodSymbol.Name (e.g. 'MessagePack.IMessagePackSerializationCallbackReceiver.OnBeforeSerialize'), never 'OnBeforeSerialize' or 'OnAfterDeserialize', so needsCast is always false; additionally type.GetMembers() misses base-class explicit implementations while type.AllInterfaces (line 83) finds them, and a single needsCast flag conflates OnBeforeSerialize and OnAfterDeserialize. Also lines 19-22 (BinaryWriteTypeFormat) in the cited 1-43 range belong to CreateMember rather than model construction.

Claim C10 disputed: None of the four named tests exercise duplicate surrogate keys (KeysMustBeUnique, lines 200-204) or unkeyed surrogate members (MemberNeedsKey, lines 171-179). In addition, line 171 accepts negative integer keys (key is int does not check >= 0), and line 190 calls IsPublicReadWrite(target) which falsely rejects public read-write virtual properties where a derived class overrides only get or only set.

Claim C17 disputed: Two of the cited analyzer doc pages make claims that contradict the implementation: doc/analyzers/MsgPack019.md line 26 states nesting types must also be partial under MsgPack019, but GeneratedFormatterCollector.IsPartial (lines 293-299) never checks containing types (resulting in CS0260 instead of MsgPack019); and doc/analyzers/MsgPack020.md line 3 states 'The class must implement exactly one such interface', but GeneratedFormatterCollector.cs line 57 only checks formatterInterfaces.Length == 0 rather than != 1.

MsgPack020's message and docs say the class must implement `IMessagePackFormatter<T>` for exactly one type, but only zero is rejected. A formatter implementing two such interfaces silently gets code for `formatterInterfaces[0]` only and then fails to compile because the other interface is unimplemented.
The existing NoDeserializingConstructor descriptor is created with no message arguments. If its message format has placeholders, the message may be malformed or fail to format. This path has no test.

In surrogate mode, every non-ignored instance property or field of the surrogate (including private fields and base-type members) must carry `[Key]`, or MemberNeedsKey fails the build. This contradicts the README wording that only the members the surrogate lists are serialized.

Only the formatter itself is checked for `partial`. MsgPack019.md says nesting types must also be partial, but nothing reports this, so a non-partial containing type produces a compiler error from generated code instead of a diagnostic.

The diagnostics pipeline combines INamedTypeSymbol-bearing records with CompilationProvider. It reruns the collector on every compilation change, and the symbols kept in the pipeline (GeneratedFormatterRequest) defeat incremental caching. Diagnostics are also reported even when source generation is disabled.
The record is declared `public` in the generator assembly although it is internal plumbing.

No test covers the body-less form `partial class X : IMessagePackFormatter<T>;` that the issue explicitly shows. Duplicate surrogate keys and init-only/required members on the external type are also untested.

Explicit IMessagePackSerializationCallbackReceiver detection is always false: in Roslyn, an explicit interface implementation's IMethodSymbol.Name includes the interface prefix (not 'OnBeforeSerialize' or 'OnAfterDeserialize'), and type.GetMembers() misses base-class implementations while type.AllInterfaces finds them. Generated formatters for external types with explicit serialization callbacks emit uncast calls like value.OnBeforeSerialize(), failing compilation with CS1061.

CreateSurrogateMembers checks 'key is not (int or string)' without requiring non-negative integer keys (int >= 0). A surrogate member with [Key(-1)] passes validation and passes IntKey = -1 into ObjectSerializationInfo.Create / FormatterTemplate, either crashing the generator or silently omitting the member from 0-based array serialization.

GeneratedFormatterCollector neither checks formatterInterfaces.Length != 1 (despite MsgPack020's message 'for exactly one data type') nor validates the user-declared formatter class itself (it can be abstract, generic, private inside a nesting type, or lack an accessible parameterless constructor). Any of these produces uncompilable generated code (CS0535, CS0144, CS0122, CS7036) in the formatter or GeneratedMessagePackResolver instead of a diagnostic.

IsPartial only checks the formatter symbol itself and ignores symbol.ContainingType, so a partial formatter nested in a non-partial outer type bypasses MsgPack019 and fails with CS0260 when EmitNestingTypesAndNamespaces emits partial outer wrappers. Likewise, MessagePackGenerator.cs line 31 filters on ClassDeclarationSyntax, silently ignoring 'partial record' formatter classes (RecordDeclarationSyntax) even though AttributeTargets.Class permits [GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] on records.

IsPublicReadWrite inspects property.GetMethod and property.SetMethod only on the most-derived IPropertySymbol without walking property.OverriddenProperty. When an external derived class overrides only get (or only set) of a public virtual read-write property, the unoverridden accessor is null on the derived symbol and the base symbol is suppressed by seen (line 267), silently dropping the property in contractless mode and falsely raising MsgPack022 in surrogate mode.

Multiple [GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] classes targeting the same T (or targeting a type that also carries [MessagePackObject]) are not diagnosed, leading either to one partial formatter being silently dropped during ObjectInfos set deduplication (causing CS0535) or duplicate type registrations in GeneratedMessagePackResolver.

Casting SurrogateType with 'as INamedTypeSymbol' turns non-named type arguments such as typeof(int[]) into null, causing GeneratedFormatterCollector to treat the formatter as contractless instead of reporting an invalid surrogate type.
